When is a project EPC+F-ready? Six questions before you approach a lender — CSM2 Finance
A project does not need to be perfect at screening. It needs a credible route to close the gaps.
When is a project EPC+F-ready? Six questions before you approach a lender
Lenders and ECAs test the same six things in every project, whatever the sector.
At screening, gaps are normal. Gaps without an owner are the problem.
Approach lenders when each open item has an owner, a deliverable and a date.

Projects tend to reach lenders at the wrong moment. Some arrive too early, as a concept with a price attached. Others arrive too late, with contracts signed and procurement fixed in a form that no export credit agency can support. In both cases the first meeting is spent discovering what is missing, and a first impression in a credit committee is hard to revise.

We use six questions to decide whether a project is ready for that meeting. They are the questions a lender, an ECA and their advisers will ask anyway. Answering them first, on the sponsor’s side of the table, turns the meeting from an examination into a negotiation.
Is the technical scope defined well enough to price and to diligence?

Capacity, design basis and scope of supply need to be fixed at a level the lenders’ technical adviser can test. A CAPEX figure that still moves with every design iteration undermines the model, the contract and the cover application built on it.
Who borrows, and what stands behind them?

Who borrows, who owns the asset, and what balance-sheet or sovereign support exists. The financing route follows the borrower: a ministry of finance, a state-owned company with a guarantee, a corporate and a project company each lead to a different structure.
A budget allocation, operating cash flow, a tariff, a power purchase or off-take agreement, an escrow arrangement. Lenders finance a repayment source. The asset is how that source is created.
Can the supply chain create eligible export content?
ECA support follows exports. The question is whether sourcing can generate enough eligible value for the intended agency without distorting the technical solution. We cover this in a separate note.
Are environmental, social, land and permitting risks on a credible path?

ECAs and development finance institutions apply environmental and social standards of their own. A missing impact assessment or an unresolved land question can stop a transaction that is sound in every other respect.
Can the contracts allocate risk on bankable terms?

Completion, performance, interfaces between packages and payment milestones each have to sit with a party able to carry them. A delivery model that leaves interface risk with the borrower is hard to finance as drafted.
The same six questions, at three points in time.

No project scores full marks at screening, and it does not need to. What separates a financeable project from a stalled one is whether each gap has a route to closure: a study commissioned, a guarantee under discussion, a sourcing plan being tested against agency rules.

We therefore look at each question in three states: where the project stands at screening, what the route to close looks like, and what must be true at financial close. The profile above is illustrative. The point it makes is general: the six areas do not mature at the same speed, and the slowest one sets the date of financial close.

The right moment is when every open item has an owner, a deliverable and a date, and when the answers are consistent with one another. A repayment source that assumes a sovereign guarantee, next to a borrower structure that assumes none, tells a lender more about the project than any presentation.
If that consistency is not there yet, the budget is better spent on closing gaps than on a roadshow.
This note sets out CSM2 Finance’s general approach. It is not legal or financial advice, and each transaction turns on its own facts.
ECA content is a structuring variable, not a procurement afterthought — CSM2 Finance
Where equipment and services come from decides which agencies can support a project, and for how much.
ECA content is a structuring variable, not a procurement afterthought
Export credit support is sized on the export contract, so sourcing decisions set the size of the facility.
Agencies apply different content rules. The lead agency and the sourcing plan have to be chosen together.
Fix the content strategy before the EPC package is locked, and write it into the contracts.

An export credit agency supports exports from its own country. That simple fact has a consequence that is often noticed late: the origin of goods and services is more than a procurement matter. It determines which agencies can take part, how large the supported facility can be, and on what terms.
For agencies that follow the OECD Arrangement on Officially Supported Export Credits, the general rules are these.
Maximum share of the export contract value that can receive official support
Minimum down payment by the buyer
Local costs that can be supported, as a share of the export contract value: 40% for Category I countries, 50% for Category II

Everything is measured against the export contract value. A project with a large, locally sourced civil works component and a modest imported equipment package may find that the supportable amount covers far less of total cost than the sponsor assumed. The reverse also holds: placing more eligible value inside the export contract can change the financing plan materially.

Content rules are set agency by agency. German export credit guarantees, for example, can include foreign content of up to 49% without special justification. UK Export Finance, in its 2019 consultation on foreign content, described a requirement of at least 20% UK content. Other agencies set their own thresholds and their own definitions of what counts.

Tenor is affected too. Since the 2023 revision of the Arrangement, the maximum repayment term is 15 years for most transactions and up to 22 years for certain climate-friendly projects. Which agency leads, and how the project is classified, shapes the repayment profile as well as the amount.
Sourcing is decided on price and technical preference alone, and the eligible content turns out to be too low for the intended agency.
Content is spread across several countries, so that no single agency has enough at stake to lead.
The EPC contract does not separate eligible and ineligible items, and every later drawdown becomes a negotiation.
Origin is assumed, not documented, and the evidence cannot be produced when the agency asks for it.

Treat content as one of the variables being solved for, alongside scope, price and schedule. In practice that means mapping realistic sourcing options against the rules of the candidate agencies before tender documents are issued; deciding which agency leads and whether others need to share cover; and writing the result into the contract structure, with a price breakdown that distinguishes export content, local costs and everything else.
The test is whether the supply chain can create eligible export value without distorting the technical solution.

The order matters. The technical solution comes first, because a project re-engineered around a financing rule tends to pay for it during operation. Between technically equivalent options, though, the one that can be financed is the better one.

Down payment, maximum official support and local costs: Norton Rose Fulbright, Recent amendments to the OECD allowing ECA to offer 95% coverage on export contracts, January 2024. The 95% figure in that title refers to a temporary OECD Common Line for sovereign buyers in Category II countries (country risk categories 5–7, with a ministry of finance or central bank guarantee). It expired at the end of 2024; the general 85% / 15% rules above apply.
Expiry of the 95% Common Line: Global Trade Review, Rearranging export finance, September 23, 2026.

Repayment terms after the 2023 revision: DLA Piper, OECD publishes revised version of Arrangement on Officially Supported Export Credits, August 1, 2023; Mayer Brown, OECD Arrangement on Officially Supported Export Credits, August 8, 2023.
German foreign content: Export Credit Guarantees of the Federal Republic of Germany, fact sheet on foreign content, May 2021.
UK content: UK Export Finance, Foreign Content Policy consultation document, 2019.

Financial close is not the finish line — CSM2 Finance
Signing the finance documents starts a second project: getting the facility drawn, on time, against documents that withstand scrutiny.
Financial close is not the finish line
A signed facility is a right to borrow, subject to conditions. It is not cash.
Each drawdown is checked against the contract, the cover and the facility agreement.
The disbursement procedure should be designed before signing, with the contractor in the room.

Financial close is celebrated as the end of a long process, and for the people who negotiated the term sheet it is. For the project it is the point at which the financing has to start working. Between signing and the last disbursement lie conditions precedent, a long series of drawdown requests and a reporting calendar that runs for the life of the loan.

In an ECA-backed facility each disbursement is tied to evidence: that goods were shipped or work performed, that the amount claimed is eligible, and that the borrower remains in compliance. The checks are not difficult. They are unforgiving of inconsistency.
Invoices that do not follow the price breakdown in the contract.
Certificates of origin or shipping documents that are missing, late or issued by the wrong party.
Local-cost claims that exceed the supported limit.
Milestone certificates that do not match the payment schedule in the facility agreement.
Variations to scope that change the eligible content without the lenders being told.
Conditions precedent treated as a one-off exercise when several are continuing obligations.

Each of these delays payment to the contractor. A contractor who is not paid slows down, and a delayed project runs up against the availability period of the facility. Problems in the back office reach the construction site quickly.
A facility that cannot be drawn is not financing.
Most of this can be prevented at the structuring stage, while the documents are still in draft.
Agree the disbursement procedure with the lenders, the agency and the contractor, and test it against a sample invoice.
Align the contract price breakdown with the categories the facility recognizes: export content, local costs and ineligible items.
Decide who prepares, who checks and who signs each document in a drawdown file.
Build one tracker for conditions precedent, covenants and reporting dates, and give it an owner.
Define how variations will be assessed for their effect on eligibility before they are approved.
None of this is sophisticated. It is the difference between a financing structure that exists on paper and one that pays the contractor on the day the contract says it should.
Choosing the financing route: start from the transaction, not the lender — CSM2 Finance
Sovereign, corporate, project or ECA-supported: the borrower, the repayment source and the supply chain decide which route can close.
Choosing the financing route: start from the transaction, not the lender
There are four basic routes: sovereign or public, corporate balance sheet, project or limited recourse, and ECA-supported or blended.
The route follows from who borrows and what repays the debt. Approaching lenders before those are clear costs time.
ECA, IFI and DFI support is an overlay on the borrower and repayment structure, not a separate world.

A common first question is “which bank will finance this?” A better first question is “who borrows, and what repays the debt?” The answers usually narrow the field to one or two financing routes, and they decide which lenders and agencies are worth approaching.
A ministry, public agency or state-owned company borrows, usually with a sovereign guarantee or a budget-backed repayment source. Appetite depends on the country’s risk and debt capacity.
A private borrower supported by its own credit, a parent guarantee, assets and covenants. Simpler to document, but limited by the size of the balance sheet.

Debt raised by a special purpose vehicle and repaid mainly from project cash flows, supported by offtake, concession rights and project-level security. Possible only when revenues are contracted and risks are clearly allocated.
Buyer credit, export credit cover, IFI or DFI participation, political risk insurance, or a mix of these, layered onto one of the three routes above.
Who borrows, and who owns the asset?
What ultimately repays the debt: a public budget, corporate cash flow, a tariff, a power purchase agreement, an offtake contract or an escrow account?
What does the country’s risk profile allow, for commercial lenders and for agencies?
Where will equipment and services come from, and which agencies does that bring into play?
What security can be offered: guarantees, assets, assigned revenues, reserve accounts, insurance?

Export credit agencies, IFIs and DFIs do not replace the borrower or the repayment source; they sit on top of them. UK Export Finance, for example, says its buyer credit facility can support corporate, sovereign and public buyers, and lists limited recourse project finance and public-private partnerships among the structures it can back. An agency changes the risk profile of a loan. It does not create a borrower or a revenue stream where none exists.
The financing route is selected around the transaction, not the other way around.
Starting from a lender’s term sheet and reshaping the project to fit it.
Assuming project finance is available for a project without contracted revenues.
Treating a sovereign guarantee as a formality, when it needs formal approval from the ministry of finance and takes time to obtain.
Fixing the supply chain before checking which agencies it brings into play.
Once the route is clear, the rest of the work becomes specific: which documents lenders will need, which agency leads, how the security package is built and how long it will take to close.

How a sovereign-backed buyer credit works, step by step
In a buyer credit, a bank lends to the buyer of exports and an export credit agency guarantees or insures the loan.
For public projects, the borrower is typically the ministry of finance or a public entity with a sovereign guarantee.
The exporter is paid against documented progress, while the borrower repays over the long term.

Many public infrastructure projects are built under a buyer credit. The contractor delivers the project, a bank lends the money to the public buyer, and an export credit agency covers the bank against non-payment. The structure separates the construction contract from the long-term debt, while keeping both tied to the same project.
Borrows directly, or guarantees the debt of a public borrower. If the ministry borrows directly, the facility is a direct sovereign obligation.
The project owner or a designated state entity, which signs the loan agreement and repays the lenders.
Arrange and fund the buyer credit facility.
Guarantees or insures the loan against political and commercial non-payment risk.
Designs, supplies and builds under the EPC contract, from the agency’s country.
UK Export Finance’s buyer credit facility is a typical example.
Maximum share of the contract value that can be lent under the facility
Minimum share of the contract value paid by the buyer directly to the exporter
Minimum repayment period, at fixed or floating rates
The public owner and the contractor agree the EPC contract, with a price breakdown and payment milestones.
The ministry of finance approves the borrowing or issues the sovereign guarantee.
The banks and the agency complete due diligence, then sign the loan agreement and the guarantee or insurance.
The buyer pays the down payment to the exporter.

As the work progresses, the exporter submits certified invoices and milestone evidence and is paid from the facility. UK Export Finance describes the exporter as being paid as though it had a cash contract.
After disbursement ends, the borrower repays principal and interest to the lenders over the agreed term.

For the Ministerial City in Cotonou, UK Export Finance supported the Government of Benin, represented by its Ministry of Economy and Finance, with a hybrid direct lending and buyer credit facility of about €121.2 million. Deutsche Bank acted as export credit agent bank, and a joint venture of Arabian Construction Company’s Benin and UK entities was the exporter.

The structure works only when every party gets what it needs. The agency needs eligible export content and acceptable country risk. The banks need cover they can rely on. The ministry needs a project that fits its budget and debt plans. The contractor needs a payment route that works during construction. The down payment, local costs and the timing of the sovereign approval are the items that most often hold up close.
A buyer credit separates who builds the project from who carries the long-term debt, without separating either from the project.

Where the contract is signed decides which agency can lead — CSM2 Finance
Export credit agencies support exports from their own country. The contracting entity and the supply chain have to be planned with that in mind.
Where the contract is signed decides which agency can lead
An agency supports exports from its own country, so the exporter’s location and the origin of supply drive eligibility.
When supply comes from several countries, agencies can share the risk through reinsurance or parallel cover.
Decide the lead agency, the contracting entity and the sourcing plan together, before the EPC package is fixed.

An export credit agency exists to support its country’s exports. UK Export Finance, for example, requires the exporter in a buyer credit to be carrying on business in the UK, and tests each transaction against its foreign content policy. Which company signs the EPC contract, and from where, is therefore part of the financing plan, not only a corporate or tax question.
Where the exporter is established and carries on business.
How much of the contract value is produced in the agency’s country, and how much comes from third countries or is spent locally.
Whether that content is documented well enough to be evidenced at each drawdown.
Country risk, and the agency’s appetite for the buyer’s market.
When supply comes from several countries

Large projects rarely source from a single country, and agencies have ways to share the risk. Under reinsurance, the agency of the main supplier covers the whole contract and reinsures the share supplied from another country with that country’s agency. Austria’s OeKB describes the main insurer as the agency of the country where the main supplier is domiciled, and allocates third-country content and local costs among the agencies in proportion to the contract value they generate. Under parallel insurance, each participant brings its own agency and the agencies coordinate. Germany’s federal export credit guarantees list reinsurance or joint insurance arrangements with a long list of other agencies.
Choose the lead agency first, based on where the largest share of eligible value will be created, then check reinsurance options for the rest.
If a contractor operates from more than one country, decide which entity signs the EPC contract with the financing route in mind.
Give the contracting entity real substance in its country: people, engineering, procurement and supply. Content rules look at where value is created, not only where a contract is signed.
Allow time. Reinsurance and parallel cover add parties, applications and approvals; OeKB notes that reinsurance premiums are payable up front.
The contracting entity is a financing decision as much as a corporate one.

Handled early, this is an advantage: a contractor with eligible entities in more than one export country can offer the project owner a choice of agencies and terms. Handled late, it is one of the most common reasons a financing plan has to be rebuilt.

A financial model is only as strong as the technical assumptions behind it — CSM2 Finance
Lenders test the engineering before they trust the numbers. Sponsors should test it first.
A financial model is only as strong as the technical assumptions behind it
Capex, schedule, output and operating costs in the model all come from technical work.
Lenders appoint an independent engineer to check those inputs. Weak assumptions surface there, late and expensively.
Review the technical basis before the model goes to lenders, not after.

A financial model turns assumptions into cash flows. The spreadsheet can be flawless and the project still unfinanceable, because the inputs that matter most, such as construction cost, schedule, output, availability and operating cost, come from engineering, not from finance.

In project and structured financings, lenders typically appoint an independent engineer, also called the lenders’ technical advisor, to review the technical basis of the project. A World Bank sample terms of reference for a wind farm shows the usual scope:
The design, the suitability of the main equipment for the site, the origin of components and the manufacturer’s track record.
Energy yield, with loss factors and uncertainty levels at P50, P90 and other probability levels.
The construction schedule and milestones, the reasonableness of the cost estimate, and cost overrun scenarios.
The EPC, supply, operation and maintenance, and offtake contracts, for technical adequacy and consistency with each other.
The technical inputs to the financial model, with sensitivity scenarios.
Permits, grid connection, commissioning and performance testing.

The same sample allows nine weeks for the first phase of this review. Findings that change capex, schedule or output at that stage change the debt size, the reserve accounts and sometimes the structure itself.
Capex built on early estimates, without a defined scope or a contingency for ground and site conditions.
Schedules that ignore permitting, procurement lead times or seasonal constraints.
Output or availability figures taken from equipment brochures instead of a site-specific assessment.
Operating costs that leave out major maintenance and spare parts.
Contracts whose guarantees and liquidated damages do not match what the model assumes.

The practical answer is to put the technical basis through a lender-style review before the model is shared: check the maturity of the scope, challenge the cost estimate, align the schedule with procurement and permits, and make sure the contracts back up the assumptions. Many advisors can build a financial model. Fewer can challenge the engineering behind it.
Lenders test the engineering before they trust the numbers.
Scope of lenders’ technical due diligence: World Bank PPP Legal Resource Center, Terms of Reference: Technical Due Diligence, Wind Power Project (sample), accessed November 2026.
The sample describes a single wind project; the scope of a review varies by sector and lender. This note is not legal or financial advice.
Six landmark financings and what they teach — CSM2 Finance
Different countries, sectors and structures, and one common thread: financing closes when the delivery model and the money are designed together.
Six landmark financings and what they teach
Each of these projects combined export credit or agency support with a clear borrower, revenue source and contract structure.
Award routes differ, from concessions to public contracts and private developments. The financing lessons are common.
Figures are as announced at the time. They show structures, not templates.

On March 16, 2018, the project company signed a financing package of €2.265 billion: a 15-year loan with a five-year grace period from 25 financial institutions in 10 countries, in eight tranches that included export credit agency and Islamic financing. About 70% came from foreign institutions. Korea Eximbank and K-SURE together provided €1 billion in loans and guarantees.
Lesson: very large packages close by combining many lenders and agencies, each sized to what it can carry.

Kalyon’s 1.35 GW Karapınar solar plant reached financial close in November 2021. UK Export Finance guaranteed a US$291 million buyer credit from J.P. Morgan, at the time its largest guarantee for a solar project, linked to GE’s inverter technology. Six Turkish banks provided about US$500 million alongside it.
Lesson: one export package can anchor agency support within a much larger financing that also uses local bank debt.

NEOM Green Hydrogen Company, an equal joint venture of ACWA Power, Air Products and NEOM, completed financial close in May 2023 at a total investment value of US$8.4 billion. This included US$6.1 billion of non-recourse financing from 23 local, regional and international banks and financial institutions, along with a Euler Hermes tranche. Air Products was the nominated contractor and system integrator under a US$6.7 billion agreement, and holds an exclusive 30-year offtake agreement for the green ammonia.
Lesson: non-recourse debt at this scale rests on a long-term offtake and a single point of responsibility for delivery.

In 2022, UK Export Finance supported the Government of Benin, represented by the Ministry of Economy and Finance, with a hybrid direct lending and buyer credit facility of about €121.2 million for a complex to house 21 ministries. Deutsche Bank acted as export credit agent bank, and a joint venture of Arabian Construction Company’s Benin and UK entities was the exporter.
Lesson: public buildings can be financed like infrastructure when the sovereign borrower, the export content and the contractor’s eligible entity line up.
Changfang and Xidao Offshore Wind, Taiwan

The 589 MW offshore wind project raised approximately US$3 billion from 25 international and Taiwanese banks and financial institutions and six export credit agencies, announced in February 2020. A 20-year power offtake agreement with the state-owned utility Taipower, and a local content plan approved by the government in December 2019, supported the financing.
Lesson: several agencies can share one project when the supply chain spans several countries and the revenue is contracted for the long term.

In November 2018, Petroperú signed a loan of up to US$1.3 billion guaranteed by CESCE, the Spanish export credit agency, with 13 international banks and a 10-year repayment term starting six months after the refinery entered operation. The financing supported the EPC contract led by Técnicas Reunidas.
Lesson: a state-owned company can finance a contractor’s scope through export credit when the contractor’s home agency is willing to lead.
A defined borrower and a credible repayment source: sovereign, corporate or contracted revenue.
An export package large enough for an agency to lead, and clear rules for the rest of the scope.
Delivery and financing designed together, with one party responsible for each major risk.
The structures differ. The discipline behind them does not.
